sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Recipients should make their key and receive secrets once
sections.para: Handing vault keys to browsers and scheduled agents by hand is slow and risky, and agents told to guard a secret sometimes refuse to use it. SG/Send's back end mostly supports a flipped design: the recipient makes a key pair, the owner encrypts and signs, the drop is read once, and the secret goes straight into the tool.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Flip the direction; pipe the secret into the tool
sections.para: SG/Send already offers one download, deletion, expiry and client-side encryption. The recipient makes its key pair, the owner encrypts to it, and the agent is told what to run rather than what the secret is. Tested end to end; the hard part is the first secret for a scheduled session.

sections.label: The pain
sections.line: Passkeys fail sometimes, and cautious prompts make agents refuse
sections.para: Browsers do not always have the passkey, and the same passkey once gave different bytes on another device. The more a prompt insists a value is secret, the more likely the model refuses to use it. The secret really worth giving an agent is its own private key.

sections.label: What SG/Send already has
sections.line: SG/Send already has most of it, except location limits
sections.para: Transfers support max_downloads, auto_delete, expires_at and client-side encryption, but there is no geographic check. The friendly two-words-and-four-digits code is only about 30 bits, and a security review of 6 August found it recoverable offline from its public id. sgit pki keygen already makes RSA-OAEP 4096 and ECDSA P-256 keys.

sections.label: The design: the recipient makes the key
sections.line: The recipient makes the key; secrets never enter chat
sections.para: An agent runs sgit pki keygen or a browser makes a non-exportable WebCrypto key, sharing only the public half, 1,164 bytes, enough for one QR code. The owner checks the fingerprint, encrypts and signs, and SG/Send holds it for one download. The recipient pipes it into sgit clone, keeping it out of the model's context.

sections.label: Tested end to end
sections.line: Decrypted once, refused twice, signature verified, key unexportable
sections.para: On a local server with sgit 0.21.0, the agent decrypted the dummy secret, the second download got 410, and the sender's own key could not decrypt it. The signature verified once the owner's key was pinned. Chromium made an RSA-4096 pair in 649 milliseconds and refused to export the private key.

sections.label: The first secret
sections.line: A scheduled session's first key is the unavoidable secret
sections.para: A browser makes its key in place, but a scheduled session starts from nothing. Either the environment holds the key, which anyone using the environment can read, making it an identity of the environment, or each session makes its own pair and is approved from a phone, like pairing a device.

sections.label: Against the trend, on purpose
sections.line: Proxies suit API keys; vault keys must reach clients
sections.para: Claude Code's network secrets and 1Password's agent server keep keys away from agents, which is right for API keys. A zero-knowledge vault decrypts at the client, so its key must arrive there. The design minimises that reach: made where used, read once, piped into the tool.

sections.label: What exists, and the name
sections.line: One-time secrets exist for people, not agent recipients
sections.para: Bitwarden Send, 1Password links, Yopass, PrivateBin, Magic Wormhole and age solve parts of this, but none is built around an agent or browser making its own key and checking an owner's signature. Handoff, KeyDrop, Courier and Baton are taken names; SealDrop is the working name, not checked in trademark registries.

sections.label: A brief for the site
sections.line: Build a separate client-first site for handing secrets over
sections.para: A site on SG/Send's transfer API with all cryptography in browser or command line. Recipients make keys and show QR codes; owners encrypt, sign and create single-download transfers; one command verifies, decrypts and pipes into sgit clone. Add pairing for new sessions, no agent passphrase prompts, no short codes, and optional location limits.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Tested locally only; the first secret remains unsolved
sections.para: The test used one local server, one dummy secret and one browser, not the hosted service. Agent refusals are an observation, not measured. The first secret is moved, not solved, other tools were judged from documentation, and the friendly code is unsafe even for a single short-lived download.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: SG/Send code and documentation for related tools
sections.para: A voice memo of 15 October 2026. The back end was read in SGraph-AI__App__Send and the flow run that day. Documentation from Anthropic cloud environments, 1Password's environments MCP server, W3C Web Cryptography API, DENSO WAVE, Magic Wormhole, age, Bitwarden Send, Yopass, PrivateBin, onetimesecret and Hermes.
